title: P versus NP
formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

importance.reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.

progress.text: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation.

Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions.

Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

status_note: The Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved, checked on 11 September 2026. The cited restricted-circuit lower bounds and proof-method barriers do not resolve the uniform decision problem.

context_blocks.text: A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.

sentences: P versus NP asks whether every problem with efficiently checkable solutions also has an efficient deterministic decision algorithm.
Boolean satisfiability is a representative test case because all NP problems reduce to it.
Checking one assignment is easy, while deciding whether any assignment works requires accounting for all possibilities.
The target concerns worst-case polynomial time on arbitrarily large inputs.
A resolution would establish a fundamental relationship between searching and verifying, without by itself determining practical exponents or average-case difficulty.
